questions.stem: A 55-year-old man was diagnosed with Mycobacterium abscessus infection. His combination therapy was to include amikacin IV .
questions.lead_in: What monitoring parameters would be most appropriate during this patient’s course of therapy?
questions.explanation: Audiology exam Aminoglycosides, including amikacin, can cause ototoxicity. Thus baseline and serial audiograms are recommended until 2 months after the final dose of an aminoglycoside.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q5

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man was diagnosed with endocarditis caused by viridans streptococcus. He had no known drug allergies. Pending availability of the minimum inhibitory concentration of the organism for penicillin, the patient was initiated on ceftriaxone IV plus gentamicin IV . Investigations: Serum creatinine 0.55 mg/dL Total white cell count 14.5 ×109/L Normal liver function tests
questions.lead_in: What gentamicin serum concentration is in the desired range?
questions.explanation: Trough concentration of 0.8 μg/mL The desired gentamicin serum trough concentration range for synergistic therapy of gram-positive infections is <1 μg/mL, in order to preserve activity and minimize risk of aminoglycoside toxicity. The desired gentamicin peak concentration range for synergistic treatment of endocarditis caused by viridans streptococcus is 3–4 μg/mL. When used for treatment of serious gram-negative infections, a typical gentamicin peak concentration range to target is 4–10 μg/ mL.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q2

questions.question: Gentamicin given once daily.

parts.text: Name two characteristics that allow it to be given once daily.
Name four indications where it cannot be used.
Define post-antibiotics effect.
Name two drugs that have PAE against gram negative organisms.

cohort_answer.text: Characteristics: Concentration dependent killing; Post antibiotic effect. Indications where cannot be used: Endocarditis, burns (volume distribution altered), obesity, pregnancy. Post-antibiotic effect definition: Persistent suppression of bacterial growth that occurs after the drug has been removed in vitro or cleared by drug metabolism and excretion in vivo. Drugs with PAE against GN organisms: Gentamicin, tobramycin, doxycycline, fluoroquinolones, macrolides

parts.text: What are two in vitro phenomena that allow for once-daily dosing?
In which body part does it achieve higher concentration than serum?
What are two areas where concentration is much lower than serum?
What genus of bacteria consistently displays lower MIC to gentamicin than to tobramycin?

cohort_answer.text: Phenomena: concentration-dependent killing, irreversible binding to 30s subunit, post-antibiotic effect, saturable toxicity. Higher concentration: Kidney (proximal tubule cells). Lower concentration areas: CSF, Eyes, Bronchial secretions, Pleura. Genus with lower MIC to gentamicin: Serratia (E. faecium typically tobramycin resistant but may be gentamicin susceptible; Pseudomonas has lower MIC with tobra than gent)

questions.question: Aminoglycosides.

parts.text: What 2 things make once daily dosing feasible
Where do they concentrate more than in the blood?
Where do they concentrate less than the blood

cohort_answer.text: Once daily dosing feasibility relates to post-antibiotic effect (PAE) and concentration-dependent (2nd order) killing kinetics. Concentrate more than blood: urine. Concentrate less than blood: CSF, biliary tree, bronchial secretions, abscess. (Anaerobic organisms lack the energy-dependent transport required for aminoglycosides to enter the cell; nephrotoxic and ototoxic - patients on aminoglycosides >2 weeks should get audiology assessment.)

parts.text: Name 2 pharmacodynamic mechanisms which explain bacterial killing and differentiate between antibacterial classes? Give two examples of antibiotics for each pharmacodynamic mechanism.

cohort_answer.text: Concentration-Dependent Killing: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin - rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; AG and FQ also have post-antibiotic effect; can be given at longer dosing intervals than predicted by half-life. Time-Dependent Killing: all beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides - free concentration maintained above MIC for a drug-specific fraction of time between doses achieves efficacy; maximizing duration of exposure (continuous infusions) leads to greater efficacy. (Alternate answer - bacteriostatic vs bactericidal: Bacteriostatic - inhibit growth/division - Tetracycline, Linezolid, Macrolides, Clindamycin. Bactericidal - kills bacteria - all beta-lactams, TMP/SMX (sometimes), Glycopeptides (weakly), Fluoroquinolones, Aminoglycosides.)

questions.question: Gentamicin Monitoring Tests (3).

parts.text: Name 3 monitoring tests for gentamicin

cohort_answer.text: Renal function/CrCl; Drug monitoring: peak; Drug monitoring: trough. When gentamicin used in endocarditis for synergy with beta-lactam or vancomycin against enterococcus/staph/strep, use 3mg/kg in 2-3 divided daily doses, target peak 3-5mg/L and trough <1mg/L; ODD should not be used given lack of data in this context (S. viridans 3mg/kg/day). Note: high-level aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci mediated by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes which eliminate synergistic bactericidal effect - should not use gentamicin for synergy in this context. Toxicity mechanisms: renal proximal tubular cells (internalization of aminoglycoside activates apoptotic pathway, subsequent necrosis of proximal tubule cells); Type 1 hair cells (target of vestibular toxicity - aminoglycosides penetrate endolymph, cochlear and vestibular tissue, apoptotic cell death in organ of Corti and vestibular apparatus). Non-biochemical monitoring: audiometry at baseline and monthly; electronystagmography; dynamic visual acuity testing for oscillopsia (loss of visual acuity of 3+ rows suggests vestibular dysfunction, prompting discontinuation and ENT referral); ototoxicity usually irreversible, can appear after treatment ends, cumulative risk with repeated exposure. Flaccid paralysis: neuromuscular blockade is rare but serious/potentially lethal, occurs when disease state or concomitant drug interferes with neuromuscular transmission (e.g. myasthenia gravis, infantile botulism, concomitant neuromuscular blocking agents, FQs, macrolides, Mg sulfate); blockade from inhibition of presynaptic ACh release and postsynaptic receptor blockade; treatment: stop aminoglycoside, consider calcium gluconate (most cases) or neostigmine (if also MG).

parts.text: Name 3 situations where once daily gentamicin is not (to be) used?
Name 3 advantages of OD aminoglycoside dosing

cohort_answer.text: Situations where ODD not used: Synergistic therapy (with beta-lactam or vancomycin for enterococci); Renal impairment (CrCl<40 mL/min, reduce dosing to q48h); Ascites; Burns >20% BSA; Pregnancy; Neonates <3 months; Morbid obesity. Advantages of ODD: Reduced cost (less frequent administration/CrCl monitoring); Ease of use; Reduced toxicity (reduced nephrotoxicity in animal studies, no significant difference in ototoxicity); optimizes Peak/MIC ratio, increases AUC/MIC ratio, utilizes PAE; comparable efficacy to traditional MDD in clinical trials.

questions.question: 16. Guy has an Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. Susceptibility testing shows it is susceptible to ampicillin and vancomycin, but highly resistant to gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: Why does the laboratory report only high level susceptibility?
b) What therapeutic consequence does high-level aminoglycoside resistance have?
c) What is the mechanism of high level aminoglycoside resistance in Enterococci?

cohort_answer.text: Only high-level resistance reported: Don't report low-level resistance since all enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides; loss of synergism with beta lactams/vanco if high-level AG resistance present. Therapeutic consequence: Can no longer use AG for synergy with beta-lactam/vanco against enterococcus, if used will lead to clinical failure/higher relapse. Mechanism: AG-modifying enzymes (N-acetylation, O-nucleotidylation, O-phosphorylation) alter the drug so it can no longer bind the 30s ribosome subunit.

questions.question: 31. Give one theoretical advantage of regimen A over regimen B based on pharmacokinetics.

parts.text: For Gram negative acute pyelonephritis: A: Gentamicin once daily, B: Gentamicin thrice daily
b) For Pseudomonas pneumonia with increased MICs, but not resistant to PIP-TAZO: A: Pip-Tazo in a continuous infusion, B: Pip-Tazo in separate doses
c) For MRSA bacteremia: A: Vancomycin thrice daily, B: Vancomycin twice daily

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin rationale: Aminoglycoside bactericidal activity is concentration dependent - higher peak/MIC ratio gives greater rate/extent of kill; goal is to maximize drug concentration at site of infection (optimum when exposure is ~8-10x MIC). Aminoglycosides exhibit a post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 0.5-8hrs). Saturable uptake in renal tubule cell/inner ear - once daily dosing gives lower renal cortical tissue concentration than divided/continuous dosing. Adaptive resistance (first exposure effect) - down-regulation of uptake after initial exposure; longer dosing interval preserves antibacterial activity. Decreases emergence of resistant subpopulations when peak is ≥8x MIC. Continuous Pip-Tazo infusion: maintains drug levels above MIC longer (time-dependent killing), better for bugs with minimal PAE. Vancomycin TID vs BID: killing depends on 24hr AUC/MIC; more frequent dosing gives higher AUC/MIC and better killing. NB. Vancomycin is cleared renally so actual dosing depends on weight/CrCl; goal trough >15 in severe infections.

questions.question: Endocarditis to E. faecalis. Sensitive to Ampi, Vanco, Genta (HN), Strepto (HN)

parts.text: Why test high-level resistance to Genta?
What is the high-level resistance mechanism at Genta?
Why is Streptomycin less preferable than Genta in synergistic treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Why test HLR to Genta: Synergistic activity between cell wall active agents and aminoglycoside is not possible in the setting of high level resistance to Gentamicin. All have low level resistance.
High-level resistance mechanism: Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes – enzyme inactivation
Why Streptomycin less preferable: AHA guidelines: Advantage: less nephrotoxic than gentamicin. Disadvantage: no published studies comparing the efficacy of regimens containing streptomycin or gentamicin; lack of familiarity among clinicians with streptomycin; higher risk of ototoxicity, which may not be reversible; drug availability limitations; most laboratories do not routinely perform serum streptomycin assays; may not have access to a clinical pharmacist to assist in dosing adjustments.

questions.question:
21. Explain the benefit of regimen (a) over regimen (b): (3)
a) Once daily dosing gentamicin vs b) Three times daily dosing gentamicin
a) PipTazo continuous infusion for Pseudomonas with elevated MIC (but still susceptible) vs b) PipTazo four times daily
a) Vancomycin three times daily for MRSA vs b) Vancomycin two times daily for MRSA

parts.text: Benefit of once daily vs three times daily gentamicin
Benefit of PipTazo continuous infusion vs four times daily
Benefit of vancomycin three times daily vs two times daily for MRSA

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin: Higher dose gives higher concentration and post-antibiotic effect, more efficient killing; gentamicin is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC); PAE up to 2-6 hours in vitro, longer with higher peak; Cmax/MIC >8 correlates with less emergence of resistance; possibly lower risk of oto/nephrotoxicity. PipTazo continuous infusion: Time-dependent killing agent, greater efficacy with T>MIC; continuous infusion maintains concentrations above MIC longest, option for Pseudomonas with higher MICs. Vancomycin TID vs BID: Better area under the curve; efficacy best predicted by AUC/MIC ratio (combination of T>MIC and Peak:MIC); AUC24/MIC targets can be met with shorter interval dosing or increased dose

questions.question: Pan susceptible Enterococcus spp.. Why do you test for HLR and what is the mechanism of AG R?

parts.text: Pan susceptible Enterococcus spp.. Why do you test for HLR and what is the mechanism of AG R?

cohort_answer.text: E. faecalis w/ AMG - bi functional aminoglycoside modifying enzyme - APH2 (HLR to gent); HLR to streptomycin can be due to mutations in the 30S ribosomal subunit and to the presence of a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

parts.text: Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

cohort_answer.text: HLAR mediated by AME (aminoglycoside modifying enzymes) - enzymatic target modification methylating the 30S subunit of ribosome; often on mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons), e.g. aac(6')-aph(2"). Streptomycin: HLR to SM can be due to ribosome alteration mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit - must evaluate for HLR separately for both gentamicin and streptomycin. E. faecium has natural resistance to tobramycin but NOT gentamicin. Use of aminoglycosides in IE varies by organism/valve type per detailed regimens (native valve GVS, prosthetic valve, SA prosthetic valve IE, enterococci, GNB IE) - can use streptomycin 15mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses instead of gentamicin, less nephrotoxicity but more ototoxicity, do not use in CrCl<50

questions.question: 20. Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

parts.text: Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

cohort_answer.text: HLAR: mediated by AME (aminoglycoside modifying enzymes) - enzymatic target modification by methylating the 30S ribosomal subunit; high level resistance commonly found on mobile genetic elements (plasmids/transposons), e.g. aac(6')-aph(2''). Streptomycin: HLR to SM can be due to ribosome alteration mutations in the 30S subunit - must evaluate for HLR to both gentamicin and streptomycin in all severe enterococcal infections since mechanisms differ. E. faecium has natural resistance to tobramycin but NOT gentamicin. When to use aminoglycosides in IE: Native valve GVS/S gallolyticus/Abiotrophia/Granulicatella added to beta-lactam as synergy to reduce to 2 weeks in highly sensitive organisms, or first 2 weeks in relatively/highly pen resistant organisms combined with Pen G or CRO. Prosthetic valve GVS/S gallolyticus: first 2 weeks in combination with 6-week PenG/CRO for highly susceptible; for pen-resistant, use 6 weeks with PenG/CRO. Native valve IE by group B/C/G strep: add genta first 2 weeks (total 4-6 weeks). SA prosthetic valve IE: initial 2 weeks genta 3mg/kg/d divided 2-3 doses with cloxacillin+rifampin+early surgery. Enterococci native/prosthetic valve IE: total 4-6 weeks with ampicillin, genta trough <1ug/ml. GNB native/prosthetic valve IE: beta-lactam+aminoglycoside for 6 weeks. Can use streptomycin 15mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses instead of gentamicin (less nephrotoxicity, more ototoxicity, avoid if CrCl<50).

questions.question: Drug shortage in a hospital.

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra respectively were not available? (give two treatment options each)
A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

cohort_answer.text: PJP (no Septra): Severe: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV, or Clindamycin 450mg PO q6h + Primaquine 15-30mg PO q24h x21d; Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID with food x21d. Toxoplasma (no Sulfadiazine): Clindamycin 300mg PO q8h + Pyrimethamine, or Atovaquone 750mg PO BID + pyrimethamine. Stenotrophomonas (no Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra): Minocycline 200mg IV x1 then 100mg IV BID, or Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO q24h, ceftazidime, colistin, cefiderocol. Streptomycin issue: high level resistance = growth in presence of high concentration of streptomycin or gentamicin, meaning no synergistic AG effect possible in vivo if resistant to both; cannot extrapolate resistance of one aminoglycoside based on the other

questions.question: Explain the benefit of regimen (a) over regimen (b) for: once daily vs three times daily gentamicin dosing; Pip-tazo continuous infusion vs four times daily for Pseudomonas with elevated MIC; Vancomycin three times daily vs two times daily for MRSA

parts.text: Once daily gentamicin vs TID dosing - benefit of once daily?
Benefit of TID gentamicin dosing over once daily?
Pip-tazo continuous infusion vs QID - benefit of continuous infusion?
Benefit of QID pip-tazo dosing?
Vancomycin TID vs BID for MRSA - benefit of TID?
Benefit of BID vancomycin dosing?

cohort_answer.text: Once daily gentamicin: convenience/adherence, less renal toxicity risk (saturable proximal tubule accumulation), concentration-dependent killing, post-antibiotic effect. TID gentamicin: can monitor trough/peak levels for PK adjustment (burns, pregnancy, renal impairment), better for synergy in endocarditis. Pip-tazo continuous infusion: time-dependent killing supports extended-infusion dosing, increasing time over MIC. Pip-tazo QID: convenience of dosing. Vancomycin TID: killing depends on AUC/MIC, allows higher AUC/MIC for maximum bactericidal effect. Vancomycin BID: convenience, adherence, less toxicity risk

questions.question: E faecalis bacteremia with a prosthetic valve 3 weeks ago. It has HLAR to gent and strepto.

parts.text: What test is required next which will impact treatment?
What treatment regimen and duration?
What's the most common enterococcus resistance to AG and how is it acquired?
Two bench biochemicals for identification

questions.model_answer: a) Next test: repeat/confirm high-level aminoglycoside resistance testing to both gentamicin AND streptomycin specifically (since HLAR to one does not preclude synergy with the other) - this determines whether an aminoglycoside can still be used synergistically. b) Treatment regimen/duration: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergy, avoids aminoglycoside toxicity) for 6 weeks (prosthetic valve endocarditis); if not HLAR to streptomycin, ampicillin plus streptomycin is an alternative. c) Most common enterococcal aminoglycoside resistance: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme) conferring high-level resistance to gentamicin (and most aminoglycosides except streptomycin); acquired via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer/conjugation. d) Two bench biochemical tests for identification: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test - positive in Enterococcus. (2) Growth in 6.5% NaCl broth and bile-esculin hydrolysis (positive for Enterococcus, distinguishes from Streptococcus).

questions.question: Post-antibiotic effect

parts.text: What is it?
Name two classes of antibiotics which exhibit this phenomenon.

cohort_answer.text: PAE = inhibition of bacterial growth following exposure to an antibiotic even after drug concentration falls below MIC, exhibited by delay before microorganisms re-enter log-growth in vitro. Possible mechanisms: nonlethal damage induced by the antimicrobial resulting in slow recovery; persistence of antimicrobial at bacterial binding sites (ribosomes, DNA gyrase) and periplasmic space. Specific microorganism-antimicrobial combination is most important factor influencing presence/duration of PAE, along with concentration and length of exposure. In human studies, aminoglycosides (extended PAE against GNB) effective with once-daily dosing. Classes exhibiting PAE: Aminoglycosides (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); Fluoroquinolones (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); beta-lactams generally do not exhibit PAE against GNB (except imipenem) but induce ~2hr PAE against GP organisms.

questions.question: 70M have AVR 3 weeks ago, now fevers/chills. Blood cultures 4/4 Enterococcus faecalis. Susceptible to ampicillin but high-level resistance to gentamicin

parts.text: What is one investigation that you would want to do, and why?
What are two microbiologic tests that would help in rapidly identifying Enterococcus?
What is the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance, and how is it transmitted between bacteria?
What is your recommended management? (2 points)

questions.model_answer: a) Investigation: transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) - higher sensitivity than TTE for detecting prosthetic valve vegetations/abscess in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis. b) Two rapid microbiologic identification tests: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test. (2) Bile-esculin hydrolysis with growth in 6.5% NaCl broth. c) Most common aminoglycoside resistance mechanism: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme), transmitted via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer (conjugation) between bacteria. d) Recommended management (2 points): (1) Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergistic therapy, avoiding aminoglycoside given HLR to gentamicin) - note streptomycin susceptibility should still be checked as an alternative synergy option. questions.question: You see a 15 year-old female patient with several weeks of fever, malaise, and weight loss. Blood cultures are positive for Enterococcus faecalis. Echocardiogram demonstrates a 1.2 cm vegetation on the mitral valve. The E. faecalis isolate is susceptible to ampicillin and aminoglycosides. She is started on ampicillin and gentamicin for 6 weeks.

parts.text: List THREE tests that should be monitored in patients on gentamicin.
List TWO symptoms/signs that may suggest gentamicin toxicity.
List TWO specific cells that are affected in gentamicin toxicity.
Name ONE non-biochemical test that may be used to identify gentamicin toxicity.
After starting gentamicin, the patient develops confusion and muscle weakness. What is the most likely cause and what is the treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three tests to monitor on gentamicin: (1) serum creatinine/renal function (2) gentamicin peak and trough serum levels (3) baseline and periodic audiometry (hearing assessment).
b) Two symptoms/signs suggesting toxicity: (1) tinnitus or hearing loss (ototoxicity) (2) rising creatinine/decreasing urine output (nephrotoxicity) - vertigo/unsteady gait (vestibulotoxicity) is another accepted answer.
c) Two specific cell types affected: cochlear hair cells and vestibular hair cells (of the inner ear); renal proximal tubular epithelial cells are also affected (nephrotoxicity).
d) One non-biochemical test: audiometry (formal hearing test).
e) Confusion and muscle weakness after starting gentamicin: most likely aminoglycoside-induced neuromuscular blockade (aminoglycosides impair presynaptic acetylcholine release and postsynaptic receptor sensitivity at the neuromuscular junction, mimicking a myasthenic crisis). Treatment: stop the aminoglycoside and administer IV calcium gluconate to reverse the neuromuscular blockade.

Vanco + Gent x 6 weeks

parts.text: a) Why do HLAR testing?
b) If susceptible, what does it mean?
c) Mechanism of HLAR in Enterococci

cohort_answer.text: a) Enterococcal endocarditis requires bactericidal regimen but beta-lactams alone aren't readily bactericidal; synergistic bactericidal effect achieved with aminoglycoside addition; synergism = >=2 log10 increase in killing at 24h compared to beta-lactam alone; gentamicin and streptomycin are the two compounds recommended; HLR defined by growth at 2000mg/L streptomycin and 500mg/L gentamicin on BHI agar (or 1000mg/L streptomycin in BHI broth); HLR to both abolishes synergistic effect; evaluation for HLR is standard of care for endovascular/severe enterococcal infections. b) Gentamicin can be used for synergy in endovascular infections. c) Aminoglycoside modifying enzyme (AME) - bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'')-Ia confers high level gentamicin resistance due to mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit.

questions.question: Give theoretical pharmacokinetic advantage of regimen A over regimen B for each scenario.

parts.text: Pt with E coli pyelonephritis: a) High dose gentamicin OD b) Gentamicin q8h
Pt with pseudomonas infection with intermediate MIC: a) Piptazo continuous infusion b) Piptazo q6h
Pt with MRSA infection: a) Vancomycin q8h b) Vancomycin BID

cohort_answer.text: a) Higher dose extended interval dosing of gentamicin achieves higher peak levels while avoiding toxic trough levels; potentially lower risk of nephrotoxicity based on animal studies (no difference in ototoxicity); post-antibiotic effect with ongoing killing after concentration drops below MIC; convenience of once daily dosing/monitoring; equivalent clinical efficacy. b) Continuous infusion: reduced mortality in meta-analysis (greater efficacy), also observed with prolonged infusion duration vs traditional dosing; can use lower total daily dose to maintain T>MIC. c) Shorter dosing interval (TID/q8h) allows target AUC/MIC to be achieved with lower loading doses, keeping peaks lower; theoretically reduces nephrotoxicity.

questions.question: Interactions between immunosuppressives and anti-infectives.

parts.text: Describe response in Tacrolimus levels in the presence of each antibiotic: Rifampin, Clarithromycin, Fluconazole
Describe clinical toxicity that could develop with each drug combination: Gentamicin + tacrolimus; MMF + TMP/SMX

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus. Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Gentamicin + tacrolimus: no true drug-drug interaction, but both can cause nephrotoxicity. MMF + TMP/SMX: no true DDI, both can cause myelosuppression.

cohort_answer.text: Lab tests: Creatinine; Gentamicin trough; Gentamicin peak. Non-biochemical test: Audiometry. Cell types affected: Vestibular type 1 hair cells; Renal proximal tubular cells. Flaccid paralysis cause: Gentamicin neuromuscular blockade. Treatment: IV calcium, supportive care
